regions.merged_text: What a consolation! What an outlook this ought to afford us! What an outstanding horizon for poor sinners -- if "hope is the very soul of happiness here" and if the revealed purpose of our creation, "TO KNOW GOD" is kept in mind, -- what a horizon for sinners if we but stop and remember that to KNOW GOD covers everything. Hence the lines: God made me to know Him. O what a bless'd aim! To love Him and serve Him sure rests in the same. Its "Heaven Begun", for the grateful on earth' To treasure aright? ! Highest Heaven its worth. But how can I know what the senses fail to perceive? How know the incomprehensible God, whose attributes -- wisdom and power and goodness and mercy -- are infinite? A simple objection may demand in the first place simple answer, and besides there is a trite proverb: "A fool can ask questions that will puzzle a philosopher to answer." A nave can ask such questions. But after all every nave is a fool too. However, a simple answer to the above objection might be to ask another very simple question: "Do the senses perceive the electricity -- "the juice"- in a live wire? Or again: Do men look at the sun itself to consider it benefits? Objections here are vain. No excuses. If the primary purpose of my creation is to know my Creator so that I may love Him and serve Him and be happy with Him; and if no one but a fool can say in his heart, "There is no God", then the necessary con- clusion would seem to be that God's existence must be manifest, one way or other, to everyone who is not a fool; consequently, that every normal person able to think can and ought to recognize his Creator -- can and must worship God; and this under pain of losing everything good in the final, and of damning his own soul -- cast out "into exterior darkness where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."
